Your typical 2023 BMW M2 has an electronically limited top speed of 155 miles per hour. However, the optional M Driver's Package raises that limit to 177 mph. According to the Arizona Department of Public Safety (AZDPS) Highway Patrol, one M2 driver was apparently determined to explore the upper limits of his car's performance before trading it in; a state trooper clocked him traveling 170 mph on the highway, and criminal charges followed.

The incident happened on November 9, 2026, on Arizona State Route 202 near Sky Harbor Boulevard in Tempe, Arizona. According to authorities, an AZDPS Highway Patrol State Trooper spotted the BMW traveling at a high rate of speed and passing other vehicles. Using a LIDAR device, the trooper reportedly recorded the vehicle traveling 170 mph in a posted 65-mph zone—an astonishing 105 mph over the limit.

Police were not going to engage in a pursuit at that speed, however, and said they decided to use the Highway Patrol Traffic Operations Center to track the vehicle's whereabouts. Eventually the BMW exited the highway, and police were then able to stop the car. At this time, the police reportedly noticed that the BMW didn’t have a license plate.

In a recent development, police say the officer asked the driver how fast he thought he was going, and the man estimated his speed at approximately 110 to 115 mph. That's still far above the posted speed limit, but nowhere near the 170 mph that had him approaching Daytona 500 qualifying territory. The driver later claimed he hadn't realized just how fast he was traveling, according to authorities.

It has been revealed that why was he driving so fast? He reportedly told the trooper he was planning to trade in the BMW and wanted to take it for one last drive. Hopefully his new car will be slower than the M2, because as police pointed out in their social media post, at 170 mph, the BMW was traveling approximately 250 feet every second. A crash at that speed would be devastating.

The driver was, unsurprisingly, arrested for reckless driving and endangerment, due to his excessive speed and unsafe driving behavior.

Leading Medical Groups Team Up to Redefine Female Heart Health

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated strategy of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.
  • The reports detail how cardiovascular health challenges can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.
  • The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quartet of medical organizations has published a comprehensive set of reports calling for a coordinated strategy of action to improve heart healthcare for women throughout their lifetimes.

The reports detail how cardiovascular health challenges can be prevented, monitored, and treated from the early years of menstruation to peak fertility age to pregnancy to perimenopause to postmenopause stages.

The report authors call for healthcare professionals to identify heart health risks early in girls and women and to coordinate care across medical specialties.

Industry observers note that they stress that females have specific biological factors that increase their risks of cardiovascular disease. Those components include hormonal and emotional factors.

The authors note that heart disease is the number one cause of death for females in the United States, as well as the number one cause of death during pregnancy. Yet, only 44% of females are fully aware of the dangers they face from heart disease.

The organizations issuing the reports are the American Heart Association (AHA), the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG), and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

The groups presented their findings in a trio of reports published in the AHA’s flagship journal, Circulation on October 26.

“Women experience their healthcare across clinical specialties, but it often is fragmented or disconnected,” noted Sadiya Khan, MD, the chair of the collaborative writing group for the reports and a professor of cardiovascular epidemiology at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago, in a news release.

“Specifically, these reports connect the dots for clinicians, for patients, and across health domains so that care is holistic and begins in adolescence, recognizing that women’s heart health is uniquely shaped by biological transitions not experienced by men — periods, pregnancy, perimenopause, and menopause.”.

Experts not involved in the reports told Healthline the updates were a long time coming.

Nicole Weinberg, MD, a cardiologist at Pacific Heart Institute’s Women’s Heart Center in Santa Monica, California, said the reports present a positive framework for women’s health.

“Women have unique cardiovascular risk factors related to pregnancy and menopause, and certain traditional risk factors, including diabetes, may increase their risk of heart disease more significantly than they do in men,” noted Nissi Suppogu, MD, a cardiologist and medical director of the Women’s Heart Center at MemorialCare Heart & Vascular Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California.

“Recognizing these differences is essential to identifying women at risk earlier, improving prevention strategies and ensuring they receive appropriate treatment,” she said.

“I am incredibly excited to see these fresh reports on women’s heart health,” added Svati Shah, MD, the president-elect of the AHA, as well as the associate dean of Translational Research and the director of Precision Genomics Collaboratory in the Duke School of Medicine in North Carolina.

“They are a call to action for increasing education, research, and coordinated clinical care for women’s heart health,” Shah said.

The organizations spelled out their recommendations in three reports.

The first report is a presidential advisory that lays out a “female-specific life course approach to the prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that “girls and women uniquely experience fragmented care” across medical fields, including pediatrics, obstetrics, and gynecology.

The authors call for a “unified life course approach that addresses the female-specific interconnectedness of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health.”.

This report breaks down the life cycle for girls and women into five stages.

“Emerging data suggest that unique biologic transitions or life stages experienced by girls and women are linked with changes in [cardiovascular disease] risk, which may be due in part to physiologic changes in sex hormones,” the authors wrote.

Weinberg said this life-stage breakdown is important, especially for risk reduction.

Industry observers note that she said complications with menstruation during the teen years may be a harbinger of heart health problems later in life. The same is true for health issues during pregnancy, especially high blood pressure or high blood sugar levels.

“We need to be aware of these heart disease risks so we’re not caught by surprise 10 to 20 years down the road,” Weinberg remarked.

Recent findings suggest that suppogu agreed. “Medical professionals should emphasize that heart health is a lifelong priority and prevention should begin early. Encourage girls and women to establish healthy habits, understand their cardiovascular risk factors, and maintain regular checkups, even when they feel healthy.”.

“Women’s heart health has a unique constellation of risk factors and manifestations that are shaped by biological transitions that vary across a woman’s lifetime,” remarked Shah.

The second report is a science advisory that recommends a comprehensive plan for women’s cardiovascular care.

In it, the authors call for a system that “integrates assessment of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across life stages.”.

They propose a “national infrastructure” of centers that would coordinate clinical care, education, training, research, and community engagement around women’s heart health.

“These centers can reduce fragmentation, enhance earlier risk identification, and expand opportunities to increase representation of women in clinical research,” the authors wrote. “In doing so, they offer a bold opportunity for a scalable and equitable model to improve cardiovascular health for all women.”.

To illustrate their point, the authors noted that only about 60% of women with hypertensive disorders during pregnancy in the United States have a follow-up visit with a healthcare professional about their condition within the first 6 months after giving birth.

“Given that pregnancy is a cardiovascular stress test and hypertensive disorders of pregnancy are risk-enhancing factors for long-term [cardiovascular disease] risk, this represents a major missed opportunity to address cardiovascular risk,” the authors wrote.

“Pregnancy and the postpartum period are crucial windows into cardiovascular health throughout the life course,” mentioned William Grobman, MD, the vice-chair of the writing group for these reports and a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at The Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, in the press release.

“An adverse pregnancy outcome can unmask increased cardiovascular risk, and that information should guide care well beyond pregnancy,” he continued.

The third report is a scientific statement that suggests a “consensus guideline for the female-specific prevention and management of cardiovascular disease.”.

In it, the authors state that there is “growing recognition that the optimal prevention and management of cardiovascular disease in girls and women requires attention to sex-specific considerations relevant to the interconnected domains of hormonal, psychosocial, and cardiovascular health across the life course.”.

The authors note several age-related warning signs of heart issues. These are spelled out in the AHA press release.

Females comprise around half the population, and their cardiovascular health “must be a part of everyday care across medicine,” said Mariell Jessup, MD, the chief science and medical officer of the American Heart Association, in the press release. “These publications give clinicians and health systems a shared foundation for recognizing risk throughout a woman’s life.”.

In a scientific statement published in February 2026, the AHA projected that 60% of females in the United States will have at least one type of cardiovascular disease by 2050.

The organization also predicted that 25% of U.S. women will have diabetes and 60% will have obesity by that year if current trends continue.

According to recent reports, the authors of that report listed several steps they mentioned could reverse these trends. Among them:.

Experts say women can also take action on their own to reduce their risks. Suppogu suggests the following:.

These recommendations can also be found in the AHA’s Life’s Essential 8 tips for a healthy heart.

“Most importantly, we need to educate women that heart disease is not inevitable, and early intervention can help prevent it and improve long-term health,” Suppogu remarked.

According to recent reports, weinberg advised women to include plenty of fruits and vegetables and a minimal amount of meat in their daily diet. She said that women should have regular check-ups with their doctor, and that adopting a healthy lifestyle doesn’t have to be complicated.

Khan said women’s health is a community effort. “All girls and women deserve more healthy years to live their fullest lives,” she said in the press release.

“Advancing women’s health is a responsibility we all share. This investment improves not only women’s health but also the health of their families and their communities.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) confiscated the orange-fronted conures during three separate operations over the last 17 months, and the white-fronted Amazons in the last several months.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past 17 months, the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx Zoo in New York City has rescued dozens of parrots from the illegal pet trade. They include white-fronted Amazons (Amazona albifrons) and orange-fronted conures (Eupsittula canicularis).

Recent findings suggest that the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) confiscated the orange-fronted conures during three separate operations over the last 17 months, and the white-fronted Amazons in the last several months. All of the birds were discovered at the U.S.–Mexico border.

“These animals were stolen from the wild and are victims of the illegal wildlife pet trade, and our responsibility is to give them the best possible chance for a healthy future,” Chuck Cerbini, WCS Bronx Zoo Curator of Ornithology, remarked in a statement. “Working with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, our veterinary and animal care teams provide specialized expertise to assess, treat, and care for confiscated wildlife.”.

When confiscated wildlife arrives at the Bronx Zoo, the veterinary and animal care teams first conduct a health check, provide any necessary medical treatment, and then help find long-term placements for those that can’t be released into the wild.

It has been revealed that white-fronted Amazons are native to parts of Mexico and Central America and represent the smallest Amazon parrot. They are also one of the few parrot species in which males and females feature visibly different plumage. Both sexes have a white foreheads, red faces, and yellowish bills, but males have red shoulders and females have green shoulders.

Orange-fronted conures, also known as half-moon conure or Petz’s conure, are also native to parts of Mexico and Central America, where they live in open woodlands, forest edges, and savannas. They have an orange forehead and green and blue feathers.

It has been revealed that the IUCN Red List categorizes both birds as a species of Least Concern, but that still  doesn’t justify trafficking them in the illegal pet trade. Parrots throughout Latin America are subject to both the loss of forest habitat and poaching.

Birds in particular l are especially threatened by trafficking because they are valued in the pet trade and the collector trade.

The most affordable Volkswagen ID. Polo Trend starts at just €24,995, or about $27,500, but you’ll have to wait close to two years to get one.

After opening orders for the ID. Polo with the 52 kWh battery at the end of April, starting at 33,795 euros ($37,000), Volkswagen made good on its promise, launching the lower-priced, smaller-battery model in July.

According to recent reports, the VW ID. Polo Trend with the 37 kWh battery went on sale in Europe in July, starting at just 24,995 euros, or about $27,500, with a WLTP range of 207 miles (334 km).

By mid-September, reports claimed Volkswagen’s entry-level EV was already essentially sold out across actross all trims, with more than 30,000 orders and a 10-month waitlist.

According to recent reports, according to the latest patch from German automotive news outlet Edison Media, that number has doubled in about two months, and buyers now face delivery times of up to 21 months for the base ID. Polo Trend. Deliveries for the sporty GTI version are expected to be around seven months.

“We clearly planned too conservatively,” a VW manager told Edison during an interview. While VW expected about 90 to 95% to choose to lease, the leasing rate is only about 50%.

The larger 52 kWh battery version has also seen higher-than-expected demand, while 90% surprisingly opted to buy the optional €810 ($890) detachable towbar.

Recent findings suggest that as a result, the company is prioritizing higher-margin models, which is likely leading to longer delivery times for the base ID. Polo.

The entry-level variants “just clog up to the line,” Volkswagen’s manager said during the recent interview.

Demand for the ID. Cross, the electric equivalent to Volkswagen’s T-Cross, is also already exceeding expectations.

The issue here is that the thing in sold out at 30,000 Units. it out to have production capacity beyond 100K!

Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT. The 52 kWh battery version will go on sale in the UK this week, starting at £30,260 ($40,000). The ID. Cross Life with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, starting at £26,985 ($35,500).

Industry observers note that volkswagen’s upcoming entry-level electric cars are off to a promising start. The electric urban car family, which includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, and the CUPRA Raval and Skoda Epiq, has received nearly 150,000 orders combined since production began in June.

However, the German automaker is still facing an uphill battle. The VW Group posted an operating loss of 5.9 billion euros ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its worst quarterly loss since the Dieselgate scandal.

In September, Volkswagen’s supervisory board approved its Future Plan 2030, which calls for reducing its global workforce by up to 100,000, closing plants, and narrowing its vehicle lineup to cut costs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Honda’s automatic engine start-stop feature is under new federal scrutiny, after the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration received hundreds of complaints that engines failed to restart automatically from a complete stop at a traffic light on certain models, prompting the agency to commence an investigation.

The federal probe, announced on Friday, November 13, includes 1.03 million units of the 2024-2026 Honda Passport, Odyssey, Pilot, and Ridgeline. The inquiry also includes 2024-2026 Acura MDX units. NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation received 701 complaints related to the Auto Start/Stop feature.

“To help improve fuel efficiency, the Auto Start/Stop system will automatically shut off the engine when a vehicle comes to a complete stop. The engine is intended to automatically restart when a driver releases the brake pedal. However, the complaints allege that the engines are failing to restart once they have been shut off by this system,” the investigation announcement reads.

Sources indicate that while automatic start-stop systems were created to improve fuel economy, Honda seems to be having a recurring glitch with the feature. Federal safety regulators previously opened a probe into Honda’s automatic start-stop system in 2025. That investigation included 2.2 million late-model Honda Pilot, Odyssey, Passport, and Ridgeline models, as well as Acura MDX and TLX units. However, the newly introduced investigation includes 2026 model-year units. Inquiry documents allege that the two issue populations have different root causes and respond differently to repairs.

There have been no injuries related to this matter, according to the feds. EPA boss Lee Zeldin mentioned the agency was investigating improvements or eliminating the technology last year; whether it sticks around in the long run, however, an engineering analysis of the stop-start system should bring Honda and NHTSA together to identify an effective solution to this recurring problem soon.

Did Darwin Kill the Meaning of Life?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • Industry observers note that when asked in school what the meaning of life could possibly be, my friends and I answered "reproduction," seeing this as the natural conclusion of the truth of evolution.
  • The strongest argument for existential nihilism has been provided by the naturalist philosopher Daniel Dennett in Darwin’s Dangerous Idea: Evolution and the Meanings of Life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

Industry observers note that when asked in school what the meaning of life could possibly be, my friends and I answered "reproduction," seeing this as the natural conclusion of the truth of evolution. As faulty as this view of me and my friends was, it was based on the view that the evolutionary "purpose" of life is essentially reproduction. This, however, is usually not what is asked when faced with the question of what the meaning of life is, or rather what makes life meaningful. What is asked for, though, is some kind of higher, eternal purpose for humans. This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.

The strongest argument for existential nihilism has been provided by the naturalist philosopher Daniel Dennett in Darwin’s Dangerous Idea: Evolution and the Meanings of Life. Evolution as a random and blind mechanism involving nothing beyond reproduction, variation, and differential reproductive success is the fundamental law of biology. Natural selection explains the origin of life and man, without any reference to purpose.

However, and from here existentialists get their name, evolution denies these kinds of essences that have "plagued" philosophy since Plato. Everything is in constant change under the blind and random mechanism of evolution. There is no essence, such as rationality or moral sense, that we could attribute to human nature. When Sartre famously remarked that “existence precedes essence,” he meant that it is left for humans themselves to decide who they are.

Industry observers note that to sum up: Evolution destroys all notions of teleology in the biological realm. Sommers and Rosenberg, in their review paper of Dennett with the fitting title “Darwin’s nihilistic idea: evolution and the meaninglessness of life,” phrase the conclusions of the Darwinian argument for existential nihilism in the following way:.

Darwinism thus puts the capstone on a process which since Newton’s time has driven teleology to the explanatory side-lines. In short, it has made Darwinians into metaphysical Nihilists denying that there is any meaning or purpose to the universe, its contents and its cosmic history.

The theory of evolution dissolves all purposes in, as Dennett puts it, “Darwin's universal acid”: science, therefore, renders God oblivious and takes away the illusion of purpose from our lives. Dennett even goes so far as to attribute the origin of existentialism to Darwin:.

Industry observers note that friedrich Nietzsche saw—through the mists of his contempt for all things English—an even more cosmic message in Darwin: God is dead. If Nietzsche is the father of existentialism, then perhaps Darwin deserves the title of grandfather.

Industry observers note that when Nietzsche proclaimed that “God is dead,” we are supposed to view science, if not as the murderer then at least as the tool that was used to kill God. While Nietzsche is often taken as a deterrent to where Darwinian philosophy leads, I argue that Nietzsche’s Darwinism is better associated with his ideas about the death of God than with the Übermensch. Even though Nietzsche is often given as an example of a nihilist, most of his work is directed against the destructive consequences of nihilism, once God has been replaced by science, or more accurately, where science left a hole after getting rid of God.

It has been revealed that especially after the horrors of WW2, it is only reasonable to ask how anyone could continue to believe that there is a God or purpose to our lives. Much of existential thinking boils down to the fact, that there is no God and hence, no one to give the universe purpose and meaning to our lives.

Thomas Nagel offers a thought experiment in which humanity realizes that the human race and our whole planet were created by some creatures to farm and eat human flesh. Clearly, he argues, this doesn’t give us the purpose we ask for when asking for the meaning of life. Would the analogy change if it was God who created us for some purpose rather than a powerful alien race? Camus suggests that this may not work either: “I know that I do not know that meaning and that it is impossible for me just now to know it. What can a meaning outside my condition mean to me? I can understand only in human terms.” Even if God exists and has some purpose for us in mind, we cannot grasp it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that one of the rarest and most coveted coins in United States history is headed for the auction block this week, where it could sell for over $2 million. But while collectors have long dreamed about owning one of the five existing 1885 silver trade dollars, the strange story of their creation remains murky more than 140 years after their minting.

The U.S. struck the first trade dollars in 1873 as a way to compete with similar silver coinage in East Asia, but the production was short-lived. Silver market fluctuations and foreign policy shifts led to their demonetization in 1876, and they were only minted for collectors beginning in 1879. By 1884, the U.S. commissioned only 10 trade dollars before finally retiring the series destroying the die casts.

Sources indicate that however, a thoroughly corrupt political appointee named A. Loudon Snowden had other plans. Snowden’s career in currencies began in 1857, when his uncle and former Treasurer of Pennsylvania hired the then 22-year-old whippersnapper at the Philadelphia Mint. While at the mint, he pursued various personal profiteering interests, including the clandestine production and selling of thousands of rare coins for collectors.In 1885, Snowden finally retired as Superintendent of the Philadelphia Mint after nearly three decades.

According to recent reports, snowden also gave himself a parting gift before retiring—five 1885 trade dollars that he purchased from the Mint cashier. No one knew of their existence until a year after Snowden’s death in 1912. The first 1885 trade dollar auctioned in 1913 for $1,140 (about $32,174 in current valuation).

Although some numismatists and historians argue Snowden’s five trade dollars were a final grift, other experts argue that the coins have a surprisingly mundane backstory. Until the 1930’s, Mint employees were legally allowed to purchase examples of new coinage for their equivalent amount. Snowden did just this when he previously bought 10 proof 1884 trade dollars, and it’s possible he bought the following year’s coins before the decision not to mint any others. Regardless of the true story, only five 1885 trade dollars exist today—and they’re worth far more than Snowden could ever imagine.

Stack’s Bowers will auction the 1885 trade dollar as part of its Rarities Night series on Tuesday, November 17.

Upgrade 11/18/2026 12:50 p.m. EST: Stack’s Bowers confirmed its 1885 trade dollar sold for just over $1.95 million.

It has been revealed that the Tudor Black Bay isn’t just any watch—it’s the perfect blend of timeless style, top-notch craftsmanship, and everyday usability. Let’s start with that 41mm steel case. If you’re ready for any action-packed adventure—007 style—the Omega Seamaster Diver 300m is the watch you want. Another bonus: Titanium is hypoallergenic, so it won't irritate the skin for people with metal sensitivities.

According to recent reports, this watch is a serious upgrade and, yeah, it’s the priciest one on the list, but here’s why it’s worth the investment: It’s a timeless classic with next-level features that will last a lifetime. In a recent development, the movement is the engine of the watch—it's what keeps it ticking. Below, we've broken down the main three types and their benefits.

Powered by a battery and known for being super accurate, quartz movement is low maintenance, lightweight, and affordable. It's a great option if you just want a reliable watch without the fuss. Quartz watches will only require the replacement of the battery every few years, which is a simple task and costs fairly little.

Backed by the motion of your wrist—no battery required. The gears that make up the movement wind themselves when the watch moves. Automatic watches feel a little more special, sometimes like high-end brands Rolex or Omega, but they'll need to be worn regularly or placed in a watch winder to stay powered. They'll also require consistent maintenance and servicing to keep them optimally running. Automatic watches typically cost more than most quartz watches, but there are many great options that are affordable these days.

Industry observers note that you wind it yourself, usually every couple days. Instead of the movement rotating automatically with motion, the gears need hand-winding to keep the movement running. These watches require attention and typically harken back to the era of vintage, throwback timepieces like pocket watches. Manual watches usually cost more than quartz watches and are on par in price with some automatic watches. They tend to be a little less affordable though.

Industry observers note that think of the case as the body of the watch—it's the shell that houses everything important, like the movement (the engine that makes it tick) and the dial (the thing with the numbers and hands). Cases come in different shapes, sizes, and materials. Below, we break down the most common materials used for cases.

Durable, versatile, and scratch-resistant. It's the most common and works for everyday wear.

Lighter than steel but just as strong, making it perfect for sports watches.

According to recent reports, scratch-proof and sleek but can be a bit pricey. It has a modern, luxurious feel.

A strap is any flexible band—made of leather, rubber, nylon, or fabric—that secures the watch to your wrist. Straps can change the entire vibe of the watch. A bracelet, on the other hand, is made of metal—stainless steel, titanium, or sometimes gold—linked together. Bracelets usually feel sturdier and add a bit of weight to the watch, giving a more premium, polished look. The good thing is many watches allow you to swap between a strap and a bracelet, so you can switch up the style depending on the occasion.

Classic, comfortable, and stylish. Perfect for dress watches but less durable for heavy-duty activities.

Stainless steel or titanium bracelets are durable and versatile for both casual and formal occasions.

Great for sports and water activities—comfortable and easy to clean.

It has been revealed that when shopping for the best men's watch, features and complications can make all the difference in terms of functionality and style. Ultimately, these details should match your lifestyle. We've broken down some crucial specs to keep an eye out for, but these are by no means an exhaustive list of everything you could find in some complex watches.

This is the ring around the watch face, and when it rotates, it actually serves a purpose (beyond looking cool). On dive watches, for example, the bezel is used to track elapsed time—turn it to line up with the minute hand before you dive, and you'll know how long you're underwater. Some bezels work for other things, like GMT watches, where they help track a second time zone. But in everyday life, most people just fidget with them because it's oddly satisfying with a ratcheting sound.

Sources indicate that water resistance tells you how well your watch can handle moisture. There are two equivalent measurements you will typically find when it comes to this rating. Meters (as in depth) is the first and atmosphere (designated as ATM and measures the pressure of every 10 meters. So the first rating is 30m, which is rated at 3 ATM. This is splash-proof, which means your watch can handle occasional hand-washing or light rain, but don't submerge it. 50m (5 ATM) is good for shallow water activities like light swimming, but no diving. 100m (10 ATM) can handle swimming, snorkeling, and most water sports. 200m+ (20 ATM) is built for diving and serious water activities. Watches like the Omega Seamaster are built specifically for this sort of pressure.

Industry observers note that A chronograph is a type of complication added to the watch movement that essentially gives the watch a stopwatch functionality. It's great for timing events, workouts, or even laps around a track. You'll typically see sub dials for seconds, minutes, and sometimes hours. While it adds functionality, it also gives the watch a sporty, complex look. The most famous example of a chronograph is the Rolex Daytona, made famous by watch icon Paul Newman.

In a recent development, A date window adds convenience—you won't have to check your phone or calendar to know the date. It's a small but handy detail, especially for busy schedules. Watches such as the Seiko 5 or Tudor Black Bay makes this feature feel seamless by blending it into the design.

Sources indicate that luminous markers or hands are a must if you strategy on wearing the watch in low-light situations, like at night or in darker environments. Watches with Super-LumiNova or tritium tubes glow brightly and for extended periods and make the dial easier to read when overhead light is sparse.

Pay attention to case diameter and thickness. Case diameter is the main number you'll see alongside watches. Generally speaking, around 38-42mm diameter is ideal for most wrists, but larger or smaller watches can suit personal taste. The diameter of cases tends to ebb and flow with watch trends. For the first part of this century, case sizes gravitated over 40mm for lots of watch makers. But in 2026, smaller watches (even down to 32 and 34mm) are en vogue. We like to find a happy medium and suggest trying on different sizes to see what's most comfortable for your wrist.

If you’re rough on your gear or are looking for an everyday wear, opt for a scratch-resistant sapphire crystal (the transparent covering that protects the dial), shock resistance, or robust designs for long-lasting wear.

Our style team, led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, continually tests almost every watch known to man and put them through their paces for everything they’re designed to handle: marathon training, cycling, traveling, hiking, sleep tracking, daily fitness routines, and dressy occasions. To identify the most ubiquitous watches, we relied on our previous experience testing and owning various models, as well as prior expert coverage on Men’s Health.

According to recent reports, we considered features such as case material, comfort, battery life, accuracy, dial design and aesthetics, water resistance, and magnetic resistance. Bonus points were given for unique specs that added functionality like a date window or sub dials. Our picks aren't just utilitarian though—they're seriously stylish, making them the perfect accessory for everything from the gym to date nights. In the end, we narrowed it down to 7 standout watches that tick all the right boxes and can provide a timepiece for any type of guy.

If you work from home, you know how much of a difference the right office chair can make. Take it from someone who's spent five years working remotely and learned the hard way that the couch isn't the best place to spend a workday. Between a standing desk, an under-desk treadmill, and monitors, outfitting your home office can get expensive. But if you're going to splurge on one piece of WFH gear, an ergonomic office chair that supports your back throughout the workday is a good place to start.

Recent findings suggest that “A supportive chair can reduce the risk of lower back pain, neck and upper back pain, poor circulation, and fatigue,” states Kevin Lees, director of chiropractic operations at The Joint Chiropractic. “This may also lead to improved productivity, enabling individuals to stay focused on their tasks without distractions from trying to get comfortable.”.

Industry observers note that to find the best home office chairs, our team consulted spine specialists and tested several popular ergonomic chairs for weeks in our own workspaces, sitting for up to eight hours a day. Our favorite is the Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro, which impressed us with its customizable support and easy assembly at a reasonable price compared to premium models from Herman Miller and Steelcase.

The right home office chair will be different for everyone, but there are a lot of factors that will remain the same, like adjustable lumbar support and thick seat cushioning. Keep reading to find which of these eight expert-recommended chairs are the perfect addition to your workday.

Recent findings suggest that meet the experts: Kevin Lees, Director of Chiropractic Operations at The Joint Chiropractic.Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care.

The Branch Ergonomic Chair Pro is our pick for the best home office chair because of its combination of comfort, adjustability, and value. At $499, it’s packed with easy-to-use adjustments that make it a steal. You can customize the seat depth, lumbar support, tilt tension, recline, and more without having to take your eyes away from your work.

After testing the chair for over a month and sitting for four to six hours per workday, WH Digital Designer Taryn Colbert gave it a five out of five, praising how easy it was to assemble and customize. In fact, she found herself using it even when she wasn't working.

“While I work, I sit it up to work on my posture,” she says. When doing her hair or playing computer games, she reclines the chair into what she calls “lounge mode.”.

According to recent reports, the armrests alone offer five types of adjustment, and you can add a headrest or a taller cylinder for an additional cost. While the mesh version has a low-key look, the leather and vegan leather options are worth considering if you want a bit more style.

Colbert’s biggest gripe was the wide wheelbase, which made it difficult to maneuver through doorways and across carpet.

Still, if you’re looking for a classic ergonomic office chair, this model is great for both first-timers and seasoned remote workers. Its customizable design is intuitive enough to use every day without requiring a four-figure investment.

According to recent reports, from the iconic Eames Lounge Chair to the ergonomic Aeron office chair, Herman Miller has earned its reputation for making some of the best seats around. At upwards of $1,500, the Aeron is certainly an investment, but you can customize practically everything, from the arm pads to the casters. It’s available in three sizes, with several options for armrest adjustability, back support, and tilt.

It has been revealed that WH Deputy Editor Eunice Lucero-Lee tested the medium-size Aeron in the Jasper colorway for two to four weeks, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. Lucero-Lee, who regularly experiences lower back pain, gave the chair a 5 out of 5.

“This had perfect lumbar support for a whole eight-hour day's work,” she states. She also appreciated the adjustable armrests and how smoothly and quietly the wheels rolled while still offering enough traction and control. (The deep forest green colorway was another bonus.).

Instead of a traditional foam cushion, the Aeron features a breathable mesh seat that offers an almost weightless feeling. And the chair arrives fully assembled—as we'd expect at this price point.

While the steep price tag was Lucero-Lee’s biggest gripe, the Aeron’s customizable fit and excellent lumbar support make it a worthwhile splurge if you spend the better part of your day at your desk.

According to recent reports, if you like to lean back and stretch your legs between meetings, the FlexiSpot ErgoX is worth checking out. Beyond customizable lumbar support, seat depth, and armrests, it features an adjustable headrest and a retractable footrest, so you can kick back and put your feet up while catching up on emails or taking a breather between calls.

WH Fitness Reviews Editor Natascha Grief, who already owns a Herman Miller office chair, tested the ErgoX for over a month, sitting for six to eight hours per workday. While she initially found the back support a little uncomfortable, it took about a week for her to get used to sitting in a more upright position.

“I think a good comparison would be switching to a pair of very supportive/corrective shoes after wearing pairs that are less structured,” she states. Once she adjusted to the chair, she liked the firm back support and how the headrest helped her maintain a comfortable neck position.

Industry observers note that grief also loved how comfortable the chair was when fully reclined, though she found the mechanism for pulling out the footrest a little clunky. She ultimately gave the chair a 4 out of 5.

Considering how many adjustments and extras you're getting for the price, the ErgoX is a great option if you prefer a more supportive seat but still want the flexibility to kick back throughout the workday.

Like the Herman Miller Aeron, the Steelcase Gesture comes at a luxury price point, but its sturdy construction, supportive cushioning, and impressive range of adjustments help justify the investment. The chair comes in different materials and colors. Plus you can customize wheels for hard floors or carpet.

Of its many adjustable features, including recline and lumbar support, the most unique is its 360-degree armrests, which allow you to comfortably position your arms whether you're typing on your laptop or scrolling through your phone.

After testing the Gesture for two to four weeks and sitting for two to four hours per workday, WH Managing Editor Laura McLaughlin gave it a 5 out of 5. She loved the firm seat cushion and how the chair managed to feel both stable and flexible.

“The back support specifically feels incredible, with firm yet comfortable padding and adjustable lumbar support,” she notes.

Industry observers note that at nearly 60 pounds, the chair is on the heavier side, and McLaughlin found it surprisingly difficult to roll around. That mentioned, she felt that its weight contributed to how sturdy and supportive it was.

The Gesture can also support up to 400 pounds, just like the Steelcase Series 2, and is backed by a 12-year warranty, which is reassuring when you're spending four figures on an office chair.

According to recent reports, if preserving your home’s interior design is top of mind, then the Branch Verve is minimalist with a unique flair and very comfortable. Made by the same brand as our top pick, this chair is $100 more and has fewer points of adjustment, but it also has a thick seat cushion and a breathable, beautifully designed 3D-knit back that comes in seven chic monochromatic looks.

Industry observers note that you can adjust lumbar support, seat depth, and tilt for a decent fit. The chair comes with an optional headrest for $59 more, and the armrests are height-adjustable as well as removable. The chair itself is on the heavier side, weighing in at 40 pounds, but it’s also Greenguard Gold certified, which means it has been tested for volatile organic compounds and chemical emissions.

For those who struggle with back pain, a supportive office chair can be the difference between a productive workday and injury. The Steelcase Series 2 is the best option for those folks because it’s weight-activated—you just sit, and the chair’s back tension adjusts to you.

The thick seat cushion relieves pressure, and you can adjust the height, width, and depth of the armrests. (Most office chair armrests are just adjustable by height and sometimes width.) The chair can also support up to 400 pounds, which is about 100 pounds more than most of our picks. In terms of design, you can choose between a variety of colors, two frame colors, an optional headrest, and wheels for carpet or hard flooring.

Sources indicate that at under $500, the HON Ignition 2.0 is a budget office chair that still delivers in terms of support and adjustability. The chair itself is lightweight and easy to maneuver at under 25 pounds, and it sports a simple silhouette that won’t be an eyesore in your home office. The armrests can be raised and widened, and you can also easily adjust lumbar, tilt, and seat depth.

According to recent reports, you can also opt to forgo armrests to bring the price closer to $400 or add a headrest and still keep the chair under the $600 threshold. The chair also comes backed by a limited lifetime warranty, which is unique for a high-quality home office chair. (For reference, the warranty on our top pick only lasts for seven years.).

At less than $100, the TikTok-famous Pukami Criss Cross Chair is a great option if you’re furnishing your home office on a budget. The extra-wide, foam-cushioned seat offers plenty of room to sit cross-legged, and its minimalist design and variety of color options make it easy to match with your home decor.

Despite its affordable price tag, the chair swivels, tilts, and can support up to 350 pounds. While it lacks the adjustable lumbar support, armrests, and wheels of our pricier picks, it’s worth considering if you work from home occasionally and don’t want to spend hundreds of dollars on an office chair.

Here are some key features to consider while you search for the best office chair for your body and needs.

Sources indicate that office chairs are not one-size-fits-all, which is why adjustability is crucial. “Adjustability lets the chair match your body so your spine stays in a neutral, supported position,” indicates Dr. Gbolohan Okubadejo, a spine surgeon and the head of The Institute of Comprehensive Spine Care. The lumbar support should match the curve of your spine, and your feet should be able to sit flat on the floor, according to Okubadejo.

Industry observers note that “An unsupportive chair, or one that does not fit properly, can lead to chronic musculoskeletal injuries over time,” Lees says. “This may lead to pain that persists throughout the day, affecting sleep and stress levels. Long-term injuries may also include nerve damage that can lead to weakness or numbness.”.

Industry observers note that most home office chairs are height adjustable and have armrests that can be raised. If a chair has a headrest, which isn’t essential, that may be adjustable as well. “Being able to tweak depth, tilt, and lumbar support prevents hot spots and improves blood flow during long sits.” Okubadejo says. “Small adjustments through the day break up static strain, so muscles don’t fatigue and posture doesn’t collapse.”.

Lumbar refers to the lower back, and supporting this curve in your spine can relieve disc pressure and keep your pelvis in a neutral position, according to Okubadejo. “Good lumbar support lowers the risk of stiffness and pain during long hours at a desk,” he indicates.

Recent findings suggest that like chair height and seat cushioning, lumbar support will vary by person. “Postural muscles start to relax after a few minutes of sitting,” Lees says. “This leads to added stress on the spinal joints and extremity joints.” Luckily, many office chairs allow you to adjust the height and curve of the lumbar support. Okubadejo recommends options that can move up and down as well as in and out instead of stationary lumbar support.

It has been revealed that the main components of a comfortable office chair are a sturdy frame, a thick seat cushion, and a supportive, breathable back. Most office chairs these days have a metal or plastic frame with a foam cushion and mesh back, although you can find upholstered and leather versions.

According to recent reports, if you have the opportunity to test chairs in person, make sure that the seat is firm enough for you. “If the cushion is too soft, it won’t offer the support needed over time,” Lees says. “A cushion that is too firm could create pressure points and possibly affect blood flow in the legs.”.

The materials of a chair can contribute to its overall weight and weight limit—both of which are important to keep in mind during your search.

Office chairs, like our top pick from Branch, can be beautiful in their own right but not necessarily as stylish as a sofa or armchair. Unfortunately, you may need to prioritize comfort over design when working from home, but you can opt for chairs with upholstery-like materials or lots of color options to marry the two.

Office chairs range in price from under $100 to more than $2,000, but you’ll find that most quality office chairs will cost around $500. It may seem like a lot to spend on a single chair, but it may also be your most-used piece of furniture outside of your bed and mattress if you work from home.

As a longtime remote worker and someone who suffers from chronic back pain, I’m particularly passionate about high-quality office chairs. When I set out to find the best home office chairs, I looked for a variety of models that would suit different body types, from height to weight. Supportive office chairs are easily adjustable, especially when it comes to seat height, armrest height, and lumbar support, so I wanted to highlight chairs that delivered on all three and beyond, with a few budget-friendly exceptions.

Losing Weight in Your 50s May Protect Your Heart Health Later in Life

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to new research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported.
  • In a recent development, charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study.
  • The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that losing weight in your 50s, even a modest amount, may help protect your heart health later in life, according to new research.Adults who lost weight in their early 50s saw their blood pressure, “good” cholesterol and inflammation change at about the same rate as adults who stayed at a healthy weight, according to a study from researchers at University College London and the University of Glasgow.Adults who gained weight in their early 50s saw those same measures worsen faster by their early 60s, the researchers reported. The authors posted the study on a research-sharing website on September 4. Other scientists have not yet peer-reviewed the work.

In a recent development, charis Bridger-Staatz, PhD, a senior research fellow at UCL, led the study. She told Healthline the main takeaway for adults over 50 was that “it’s not too late to try and do things that are going to improve your health.”Nearly half of U.S. adults ages 40 to 59 had obesity from 2021 to 2023, the highest rate of any adult age group, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Among all U.S. adults, around 31.7% were overweight, according to the CDC.

The findings can apply to Americans because British and U.S. adults share similar weight patterns, mentioned Solveig Cunningham, PhD, a professor of global health at Emory University’s Rollins School of Public Health. Cunningham, who was not involved in the research, told Healthline that Americans tend to gain weight across adulthood.

In a recent development, “By the time you get into your 50s, close to the majority of Americans already have obesity. Many others have overweight,” she said.The World Health Organization (WHO) calls obesity a chronic disease. Healthcare professionals diagnose overweight and obesity using a person’s weight and height, or body mass index (BMI).

Bridger-Staatz remarked the team set out to learn who lost weight and kept it off before GLP-1 weight loss medications became available, and whether that weight loss improved health over time.

She stated researchers had long assumed that “once people had become overweight or developed obesity, people didn’t really lose weight and certainly not sustained it.”The team also asked, she said, “can we try and say something positive about health that isn’t just this kind of like doom and gloom?”The researchers used the British 1958 National Child Development Study, which has followed about 17,500 people born during one week in 1958. Of those, 6,309 took part in a health check in their early 60s, according to the report.The team compared each person’s highest weight between ages 23 and 42 with their weight between ages 50 and 55. Researchers sorted people by whether they gained or lost more than 5% of their body weight and kept the change. For a 200-pound person, 5% equals 10 pounds.To track heart health, the team compared blood tests and blood pressure readings at ages 44 and 62 with those of people who maintained a healthy weight.“We know everyone’s heart health is kind of going to get a little bit worse over that time because you are aging and that’s expected,” Bridger-Staatz said. The question, she said, was, “Does it slow the rate at which people’s heart health is getting worse?”.

In a recent development, weight loss slowed the decline in heart health for people who were overweight and for people with obesity, according to the report.People who were overweight and lost weight had the strongest positive results. By age 62, their body fat-to-lean tissue ratio matched that of the healthy-weight group. The authors wrote that differences in body fat may partly explain why weight changes affected heart health.People with obesity who lost weight had less body fat at 62 than people in the other obesity groups, according to the report.Sudhakara Chennareddy, MD, prevention cardiologist in the Center for Cardiovascular Prevention, Metabolism and Lipids at Georgia Heart Institute, told Healthline those results are what he’d expect. He was not involved in the research.“Even losing 5% has beneficial effects on the cardiovascular side effects,” he noted. Long-term blood sugar was the exception. For people with obesity who lost weight, it rose more than in the healthy-weight group, though the authors reported that the result was not statistically significant.

According to recent reports, A 2025 study of more than 15,000 U.S. adults, published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Metabolism, found that adults who had previously had obesity tended to have higher blood sugar than those who had never had it, even after their BMI dropped.

“It’s not the patient’s fault… We need to treat this one like any other chronic disease, like we treat hypertension or we treat diabetes,” Chennareddy said.Compared with the healthy-weight group, people who gained weight in their early 50s had faster increases in blood pressure, blood fats, and inflammation, and declines in “good” cholesterol. Obesity is a chronic metabolic disease that leads to inflammation in the body, which can raise the risk of heart attack and stroke and worsen cholesterol levels, Chennareddy said. “The more weight they gain, they develop prediabetes and diabetes and fatty liver disease as well,” he said.These changes were largest for people who developed obesity or already had obesity and gained more weight, the researchers reported. This group also saw faster increases in long-term blood sugar levels.About 37% of participants gained more than 5% of their body weight in their early 50s. Only about 6% lost weight and kept it off, according to the study.“To me, that’s sort of the stronger message,” Cunningham said of the findings. Her advice for adults in their 50s is to avoid gaining weight.

People with obesity who lost and then gained the weight back saw faster drops in “good” cholesterol and faster rises in inflammation and long-term blood sugar.

By age 62, they weighed slightly less, on average, than people whose obesity remained steady, according to the report’s data. They also carried more body fat and had more inflammation.Weight cycling can do more harm than steady weight, Chennareddy stated. He gave the example of someone who gains 20 pounds, loses 30 and then gains 20 again. “That is even more detrimental,” he said.When people lose weight, the body slows its resting metabolism, he said. When the weight comes back, “most of the weight they gain is fat, not muscle,” he said. Even someone who loses and regains 5% to 7% of their body weight may end up with slightly less muscle and more fat, he said.Some research has shown that weight fluctuation is associated with a higher risk of high blood pressure and cardiovascular disease-related death.

The study’s weight changes took place between about 2008 and 2013, according to the study’s timeline.

Sources indicate that wegovy, a GLP-1 medication for weight management, launched in the United Kingdom in September 2023, according to the UK Department of Health and Social Care.Cunningham noted the weight-cycling findings raised questions for people who take GLP-1 medications. She said drugmakers’ own data show that “once you get off of those, your weight is going to go right back to where it was before, possibly even worse.”That could create the same up-and-down pattern, Cunningham said. She added that researchers don’t yet know “what happens in the really long term” for people who take these medications.

The study highlighted links between weight changes and heart health and cannot prove that weight changes caused the results, according to the authors. They wrote that the small number of people who lost weight made those results less precise.Bridger-Staatz also mentioned the team did not look at why or how people lost weight.

Cunningham noted adults lose muscle and bone mass with age, and that the loss is especially pronounced for women in their 50s and older. “Maintaining muscles and maintaining bones is so, so key,” she said.Staying active helps people keep muscle, even without weight loss, Cunningham said. “Even a little bit of activity…just keep moving,” she said.GLP-1 medications work best as part of a “comprehensive strategy,” Chennareddy said. With his patients, he said he recommends continuous improvement rather than setting a goal to lose a specific amount of weight within a set period.Patients who treat weight loss as “a gradual process” do better long term, he said.“The most important thing is not to do fad diets,” Chennareddy said.For people losing weight, Chennareddy recommended:.

Anyone considering changes to their weight can talk with a healthcare professional about their weight history and goals.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk once promised the fully autonomous, steering-wheel- and pedal-free Tesla Cybercab would arrive before the year 2027, and start at less than $30,000. Prominent tech influencer Marques Brownlee promised back in 2024 to shave his head if Tesla delivered on that cost and timeline. It has been revealed that cybercab pricing starts at $29,990, a price that includes the first month of the autonomy subscription required to operate the vehicle; every subsequent month, however, users will need to pay $299 for that subscription. Customers can reserve a Cybercab with a non-refundable $1000 deposit. Deliveries in Austin, Texas will begin in December 2026.

But, as the saying goes, there’s a catch. The first one here is that owners can only operate the Tesla Cybercab in areas where it has been approved for use. According to Tesla’s website, that currently includes major cities in two states: Austin, San Antonio, Dallas-Fort Worth, and Houston in Texas, and Tampa Bay, Orlando, and Miami in Florida. Tesla’s website lists Las Vegas, Phoenix, and Jacksonville as “coming soon.”.

Another restriction is that Tesla is not selling the Cybercab to fleet operators—the most obvious customer—just yet. Customers in this initial batch may purchase one Cybercab, and only for personal use. However, Tesla does have an interest form that potential fleet operators can fill out on its website.

Recent findings suggest that the Cybercab and autonomous driving in general represent potentially game-changing technology—a major reason automakers and major tech companies have invested heavily and worked on it for more than a decade. In theory, Tesla and third-party operators could offer incredibly low ride-sharing prices, with no driver who needs to be compensated with humane wages. Prices would be low enough not just to undercut rideshare providers such as Uber and Lyft, but potentially to undermine personal vehicle ownership itself.

But achieving that Tesla-driven utopia may be a far-off prospect. To change the game, the technology must work. As Jeremy Clarkson and others have noted, Tesla’s Cybercab ride-sharing service still has several kinks to work out. Broad regulatory approval remains a relatively distant prospect. And even if the technology works and meets safety standards, customers still have to buy in.

#18122. Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data demonstrates a speed problem

Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data demonstrates a speed problem

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1170 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.
  • Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph.
  • The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

The first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:.

Those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

According to recent reports, the second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”.

There are four of them, all in September 2026:.

It has been revealed that tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

The Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

Sources indicate that tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

Industry observers note that two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

Industry observers note that across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider said they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Recent findings suggest that those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

It has been revealed that the Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

In the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:.

Industry observers note that engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

It has been revealed that the Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

Sources indicate that what the data highlights is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

Sources indicate that to be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data highlights at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

But it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

Internet-famous bald eagle Shadow has endured an up-and-down 2026. From suffering the loss of a clutch of eggs to welcoming two chicks, and from losing his longtime partner to finding a newly introduced friend, he’s had a tumultuous year.

Eagles will typically defend their nest from intruders so Shadow’s willingness to share his space with an eagle other than Kaydee surprised many viewers.

Shadow returned the nest solo later in the afternoon as the sun set over Significant Bear Lake.

According to recent reports, as this is nature, all we can do is sit back and see what unfolds. Mating season is approaching, so we have to wait and see if Shadow selects a new partner. Female eagles in Substantial Bear Valley typically lay their first clutch of eggs in January. Flying around Major Bear is completely normal behavior for young adult eagles at this time of year.

Industry observers note that in January, Jackie laid two eggs in the nest, but ravens destroyed them. She later laid two more eggs that hatched in April and named Luna and Sandy. The name Sandy is in honor of FOBBV’s former executive director Sandy Steers who died from cancer in February.

Her packed cell volume (PCV) fell below six percent, before rising to nine percent. Jackie died early in the morning on August 10. #18120. The Most Dangerous Compliment You Can Receive

The Most Dangerous Compliment You Can Receive

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.
  • In a recent development, we have probably all met someone along the way who impressed and attracted us with their charm, charisma, and positive attention.
  • Recent findings suggest that in the course of my almost 30 years as a prosecutor, I have observed one of the most seductive techniques used by sexual predators and human traffickers to be targeting young women who are not used to receiving positive attention.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan.

In a recent development, we have probably all met someone along the way who impressed and attracted us with their charm, charisma, and positive attention. Yet at times, they may have made us feel unsettled with their praise. Their flattery may have been enjoyable at the beginning, but over time, some of the compliments may have gone over the top and made us uncomfortable. From our “stunning” appearance to our “brilliant” intellect, the acclaim was unmerited and even arguably untrue. What is their motivation? Research investigates this question.

Recent findings suggest that in the course of my almost 30 years as a prosecutor, I have observed one of the most seductive techniques used by sexual predators and human traffickers to be targeting young women who are not used to receiving positive attention. Having grown up in the shadow of much prettier peers and classmates, they are uniquely vulnerable to the unmerited compliments and advances of handsome (usually much older) men. Yet this dynamic is not limited to criminal perpetrators; it is used in everyday life by people seeking to manipulate and exploit people and resources.

Benjamin A. Rogers et al. (2023) discussed the impact of praise in a study entitled, “Too Naïve to Lead: When Leaders Fall for Flattery.”[1] They identify flattery as one of the “oldest and most commonly used” tactics of impression management, one that frequently benefits the flatterer. Yet flattery also impacts the recipient, who may reward the praise, inadvertently compromising their perception. Managers are apparently not immune from this dynamic, as Rogers et al. note that when they reward flatterers, they risk being viewed as naïve. And “falling for flattery” can compromise impressions of both leaders and the organizations they represent.

Yet if you know what to look for, you can detect it.

As a practical matter, false compliments often target idealized traits you would love to have but know you do not. A false flatterer will comment on your gorgeous figure or uncanny knack for solving complex problems—with very little or no evidence to support their compliments. In such instances, motivation is inherently suspect. “What do you want?” you might ask jokingly, when, actually, that is a very good question. Because many compliments are paired with an “ask,” requesting us to do something for the praise-giver, which puts their motivation under greater scrutiny. This is especially suspect when your denial of the request is met with hostility or expressions of disappointment.

The more challenging example is when you receive compliments in borderline areas where you may indeed possess some degree of the appearance or aptitude alleged. Here, we wonder whether our vocal admirer is merely viewing us with positive bias through rose-colored glasses. Yet if that is the case, they are unlikely to include a request, and certainly not become hostile or rude when we refuse.

Recent findings suggest that another red flag is mixing praise with criticism. This method of manipulation is designed to make us unsteady and anxious, leading some people to feel the need to behave in a certain way in order to be rewarded with flattery, instead of disheartened by criticism.

So, whether you are the boss or a new employee, a friend or potential paramour, keep your emotional antenna up both professionally and personally, and receive praise responsibly.

Tech Report: How to Do the Walking Lunge for Lower Body Gains

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that YOUR LEGS ARE built for movement, whether you’re running, walking, or jumping.
  • Enter the walking lunge, a truly dynamic lower-body exercise that’s a perfect complement to exercises like heavy squats and Romanian deadlifts.
  • Walking lunges might appear deceptively simple at first, especially if you have done standard reverse lunges before.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that YOUR LEGS ARE built for movement, whether you’re running, walking, or jumping. So why do most go-to leg exercises have you planting your feet in one spot?

Enter the walking lunge, a truly dynamic lower-body exercise that’s a perfect complement to exercises like heavy squats and Romanian deadlifts. (A bonus: It’s a unilateral exercise that isn’t the dreaded Bulgarian split squat.) The walking lunge is one of the few strength moves that truly gets you moving. And in doing so, it exposes muscle imbalances, trains balance and coordination, and challenges your core and upper body more than you might expect—all while attacking every muscle in your legs.

Walking lunges might appear deceptively simple at first, especially if you have done standard reverse lunges before. And in truth, they can be simple. Here, Men’s Health fitness director Ebenezer Samuel, C.S.C.S. walks you through the steps to take so that you’re not dragging your feet but making gains toward powerful legs.

FORM IS EVERYTHING with this move. You’ll want to stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, squeeze your glutes and shoulder blades while keeping your gaze at a neutral spot straight ahead of you.

Once you’re comfortable with this slow and controlled movement, you can add weights to build extra muscle and strength. You can hold them at your sides, hold them by your shoulders in what’s called a front rack position, or grab one heavy dumbbell and hold it to your chest in a goblet position. “Regardless of how you hold the load, make sure to keep your upper-body tight,” indicates Samuel. “Grip the dumbbells like you mean it, squeeze your shoulder blades, and tighten your abs, too.”.

Recent findings suggest that don’t obsess over keeping your torso too upright, though, says Samuel. “Especially as you work with heavier loads, don’t be afraid to lean forward slightly,” he says. “That can help you capitalize on your glutes, one of your strongest muscle groups, with each stride.”.

In a recent development, when you’re starting out, notes Samuel, aim to take a step that keeps your front shin perpendicular to the ground when you lower your torso into the lunge. But as you grow more experienced, you can play with the length of your stride to chase different goals. “If you take very small steps forward,” says Samuel, “you’ll attack your quads more. Larger steps can help you build hip mobility and knee health. If you take larger steps, go lighter with the load.”.

According to recent reports, “The greatest benefits of the walking lunge come from how it challenges us while in motion,” says Samuel. “In addition to building strength and muscle, every step forward challenges your front leg (primarily tibailis and quad muscles) to decelerate your body in space, and then promptly work to accelerate into the next step. That’s building coordination and balance, in addition to training almost every lower-body muscle and building serious strength.”.

You’ll work a number of major leg muscles when you do walking lunges, including your calves, hamstrings, quads, and glutes.

SMALL MISTAKES IN your walking lunge technique can turn the lower body exercise into a potential knee-wrecking disaster.

According to recent reports, you want to land on the heel of your foot first to provide a strong base for the rest of your lunge position. When you get started with walking lunges, aim for a vertical shin as you lower down to the ground to stay at a 90-degree angle in your front and back legs.

You also don’t want to think of taking a step forward, but stepping out a couple inches by slightly turning your glute. Another adjustment to protect your knee is to shift your knee slightly outward instead of toward the midline. (If you still feel any knee pain during lunges, try a reverse lunge instead).

Keep your torso straight and avoid dipping forward, which you may be more inclined to do if you’re carrying heavy weights for this exercise. Your chest should be aligned with the back of your thigh the entire time. As you get up from the lunge, you want to avoid using momentum. That means no shoulder or torso rocking.

It has been revealed that THE WALKING LUNGE is a great way to sneak in some movement on leg day if most of your lower-body exercises have both feet anchored to the ground. Load up some weights, and try to aim for 3 sets of 8 to 10 reps per leg, 1 to 2 times a week. You can alternate each leg or finish up all your reps on one leg before switching to the other. Samuel says that will keep more tension and gives you an opportunity to really focus on the muscle.

Industry observers note that an advantage of this move is its versatility, allowing you to do it anytime, anywhere. If you’re crunched for time or in a hotel room, try bodyweight walking lunges. Do it for 45 seconds with a 15 second rest for 5 minutes to break a sweat and build muscle.
